section.title: Offerings for the Appointed Feasts
section.sectionRationale: Continuing the offering calendar begun in chapter 28, this chapter completes the year with the great autumn feasts: the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the seven, then eight, days of the Feast of Tabernacles. Together these close out Israel's worship calendar just before the record turns to vows, war, and the settlement of the land.
section.thesis: The LORD prescribes offerings for the Feast of Trumpets, the solemn day of humbling on the tenth of the seventh month, and the extended Feast of Tabernacles, with its decreasing bulls each day and a closing eighth-day assembly, completing the yearly rhythm of worship that anchors Israel's national life to God.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the Feast of Trumpets on the first day of the seventh month; the solemn day of humbling and atonement on the tenth day; and the seven days of the Feast of Tabernacles with its closing eighth-day assembly.

units.label: The Feast of Trumpets
units.note: a day to sound the trumpets

verses.text: “On the first day of the seventh month, you are to hold a sacred assembly, and you must not do any regular work. This will be a day for you to sound the {{trumpets|trumpets}}.
As a pleasing aroma to the LORD, you are to present a burnt offering of one young bull, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
together with their grain offerings of fine flour mixed with oil, three-tenths of an ephah with the bull, two-tenths of an ephah with the ram,
and a tenth of an ephah with each of the seven male lambs.
Include one male goat as a sin offering to make atonement for you.
These are in addition to the monthly and daily burnt offerings with their prescribed grain offerings and drink offerings. They are a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD.

units.label: The tenth day: humbling and atonement

media.alt: A solitary altar under a still sky on the tenth day of the seventh month
media.caption: A sacred assembly, a day to humble the soul before the LORD.

verses.text: On the tenth day of this seventh month, you are to hold a sacred assembly, and you shall {{humble|humble yourselves}}; you must not do any work.
Present as a pleasing aroma to the LORD a burnt offering of one young bull, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
together with their grain offerings of fine flour mixed with oil, three-tenths of an ephah with the bull, two-tenths of an ephah with the ram,
and a tenth of an ephah with each of the seven lambs.
Include one male goat for a sin offering, in addition to the sin offering of atonement and the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offerings.

units.label: The Feast of Tabernacles begins
units.note: a feast to the LORD for seven days

verses.text: On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, you are to hold a sacred assembly; you must not do any regular work, and you shall observe a feast to the LORD for seven days.
As a pleasing aroma to the LORD, you are to present an offering made by fire, a burnt offering of thirteen young bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with the grain offering of three-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil with each of the thirteen bulls, two-tenths of an ephah with each of the two rams,
and a tenth of an ephah with each of the fourteen lambs.
Include one male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.

units.label: The seven days of the feast

verses.text: On the second day you are to present twelve young bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs, according to the number prescribed.
Include one male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.
On the third day you are to present eleven bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs, according to the number prescribed.
Include one male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.
On the fourth day you are to present ten bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs, according to the number prescribed.
Include one male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.
On the fifth day you are to present nine bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs, according to the number prescribed.
Include one male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.
On the sixth day you are to present eight bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs, according to the number prescribed.
Include one male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.
On the seventh day you are to present seven bulls, two rams, and fourteen male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs, according to the number prescribed.
Include one male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.

units.label: The eighth day and closing summary
units.note: just as the LORD had commanded

verses.text: On the eighth day you are to hold a solemn assembly; you must not do any regular work.
As a pleasing aroma to the LORD, you are to present an offering made by fire, a burnt offering of one bull, one ram, and seven male lambs a year old, all unblemished,
along with the grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs, according to the number prescribed.
Include one male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the regular burnt offering with its grain offering and drink offering.
You are to present these offerings to the LORD at your appointed times, in addition to your vow and freewill offerings, whether burnt offerings, grain offerings, drink offerings, or peace offerings.”
So Moses spoke all this to the Israelites just as the LORD had commanded him.

trumpets.gloss: A shout or trumpet blast, an alarm. The Feast of Trumpets marked the start of the seventh month with a sound meant to gather Israel's attention and call the nation to renewed remembrance before God, later becoming the basis for the Jewish new year, Rosh Hashanah.

humble.gloss: To humble, to afflict oneself. This tenth-day command to humble the soul, understood in Leviticus 16 and 23 as fasting and repentance, marks this as Israel's most solemn day, the Day of Atonement, when the nation's sins were symbolically covered before the LORD.

basic.context: This chapter completes the yearly worship calendar begun in the previous one, covering the autumn feasts: a trumpet blast calling Israel to attention on the first of the seventh month, a solemn day of humbling and atonement on the tenth, and an extended, joyful seven-day (then eight-day) Feast of Tabernacles closing out the sacred year.
basic.hermeneutics: This is detailed ceremonial law establishing Israel's national religious calendar, not primarily moral instruction for individual readers. Its purpose is to structure an entire year of corporate worship around remembrance, repentance, and celebration before God.
basic.originalLanguages: The teruah, trumpet blast, opens the seventh month with an alarm calling Israel to attention. Ten days later comes the day Israel must anah, humble or afflict, themselves, a solemn day of national repentance later called the Day of Atonement, before the year closes with the joyful, decreasing-sacrifice rhythm of the Feast of Tabernacles.
basic.typology: The steadily decreasing number of bulls across the seven days of Tabernacles, from thirteen down to seven, some later Jewish tradition read as representing the nations of the world, gradually diminishing, while Israel's own eighth-day assembly stood alone and complete, a picture some Christian readers connect to the ingathering of the nations ultimately fulfilled in Christ's kingdom.
basic.christ: The Day of Atonement's sin offering, repeated here as throughout Israel's worship, anticipates the once-for-all atonement Christ accomplishes; Hebrews contrasts the yearly repetition of such offerings with Christ's single sacrifice, which need never be repeated because it fully and finally deals with sin, Hebrews 9:25-26.
basic.god: God structures even Israel's most joyful national festival, Tabernacles, around continued sin offerings, showing that celebration before Him never bypasses the reality of sin; yet He also ordains genuine, extended joy, seven full days of feasting, showing that atonement and celebration belong together rather than in opposition.
basic.crossReferences: Leviticus 16 and 23 supply the fuller instructions for the Day of Atonement and Feast of Tabernacles that this chapter assumes. Hebrews 9:25-26 contrasts the yearly repeated Day of Atonement offering with Christ's single, sufficient sacrifice. John 7:37-38 has Jesus speaking on the last, greatest day of this very feast, offering Himself as the living water it anticipated.
basic.oneStory: Israel's sacred year moves from alarm, to humbling, to joyful celebration, a rhythm of repentance and gladness held together rather than separated. That same rhythm finds its full and final meaning in Christ, whose once-for-all atonement fulfills the Day of Atonement's endless repetition, and whose living water answers the very feast John records Him addressing directly.

context.literary:
Numbers 28 and 29 form a single speech, opened by the charge of Numbers 28:2 to present God's food 'at its appointed time' and closed by the summary of Numbers 29:39 and the note of obedience in verse 40. Chapter 28 laid down the daily lambs, the Sabbath, the new moon, Passover with Unleavened Bread, and the Feast of Weeks. Chapter 29 is given wholly to the seventh month, which receives more festival sacrifices than any other month of the year.

The chapter moves in four panels: the first day, verses 1 to 6; the tenth day, verses 7 to 11; the seven days beginning on the fifteenth, verses 12 to 34; and the eighth day, verses 35 to 38. Each panel follows the same order: the date, the sacred assembly and the rest from work, the burnt offering, the grain offering measured by the tenth of an ephah, the male goat for a sin offering, and a closing note that all this comes 'in addition to' what was already required.

The repetition is the point. Across verses 17 to 34 the paragraph is written out six more times, and only the number of bulls changes, twelve, eleven, ten, nine, eight, seven. The listener hears a countdown. On the seventh day the count reaches seven, and on the eighth the pattern breaks back to one bull, one ram and seven lambs, the same set offered on the first and tenth days, verses 2, 8 and 36. Those single bull days bracket the whole month.

Verse 39 then mentions 'your vow and freewill offerings,' and that phrase is the hinge into chapter 30, which takes up the law of vows. In the Hebrew Bible verse 40 is counted as the first verse of chapter 30, which shows how closely the two were joined.
context.historical:
The seventh month fell in early autumn, at the close of the agricultural year, when grapes and olives had been gathered and the threshing was done. Exodus 23:16 calls Tabernacles 'the Feast of Ingathering at the end of the year,' and Exodus 34:22 places it 'at the turn of the year.' Before the exile the month was called Ethanim, 1 Kings 8:2; the later name Tishri, used in Jewish tradition, does not appear in Scripture.

These laws were given on the plains of Moab to a generation that had never yet gathered a harvest of its own. Forty years of manna lay behind them. A calendar built around produce, flour, oil and wine was itself a promise that they would soon have fields.

The scale was vast. Over the eight days of Tabernacles the chapter requires seventy one bulls, fifteen rams and one hundred and five lambs, together with eight goats, before counting the daily offerings and any private gifts. Only a settled people with herds and a central altar could sustain it, which is why Deuteronomy 16:15 ties the feast to 'the place He will choose.'

The month was remembered at key moments of Israel's history. Solomon dedicated the temple at this feast, 1 Kings 8:2 and 2 Chronicles 7:8-10. The returned exiles rebuilt the altar and restarted the offerings on the first day of the seventh month, Ezra 3:1-6, and under Ezra the law was read on the same date and the booths rebuilt, Nehemiah 8:2 and 8:14-18. Later Jewish practice in the Second Temple period, described in the Mishnah, added a daily water pouring and great lamps in the temple courts, the setting in which John places the feast of John 7.
context.canonical:
The chapter is one of four calendars in the Torah. Exodus 23:14-17 names the three pilgrim feasts; Leviticus 23 sets out all the appointed times with their rest and meaning; Deuteronomy 16 stresses the central sanctuary and the joy of the whole household. Numbers 28 and 29 supply what the others leave out, the exact count of animals, flour, oil and wine, so that the priests would know what each day required.

The Day of Atonement of verses 7 to 11 assumes the rite of Leviticus 16, with its two goats and the entry of the high priest behind the veil, and verse 11 refers to that separate 'sin offering of atonement.' Isaiah 58:3-7 later rebukes a people who fasted on such days while oppressing their workers. Acts 27:9 still dates a voyage by 'the Fast.'

Tabernacles runs through the rest of the canon. Solomon's great assembly on the eighth day is recorded in 2 Chronicles 7:9. Ezra 3:4 says the returned exiles offered 'burnt offerings daily based on the number prescribed for each day,' a clear echo of this chapter. Hosea 12:9 threatens and promises a return to tents 'as in the days of the appointed feast,' and Zechariah 14:16 sees the nations going up 'to celebrate the Feast of Tabernacles.'

In the New Testament, John 7 is set at this feast, and Jesus speaks on 'the last and greatest day,' John 7:37. Hebrews 9 and 10 read the yearly Day of Atonement as a shadow now fulfilled, and Revelation 7:9-17 pictures a great multitude with palm branches, sheltered by God who 'will spread His tabernacle over them.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses records these figures for a people about to enter the land so that their worship would be ordered by God's word and not by their own taste. The steady 'you are to present' of each paragraph teaches that Israel did not invent its feasts or decide how much to give. God set the times, and God set the measure.

The arithmetic also carried a message. By giving the seventh month more sacrifices than any other, the chapter taught that the climax of Israel's year was a month of being gathered before God: called by a trumpet, cleansed on the tenth day, and then feasting in His presence for a week and a day. The first hearers were meant to see that joy and cleansing belong to the same month and the same altar.

The repeated goat of the sin offering on every single day, even in the week of rejoicing, was a lesson in itself. Israel was to rejoice as a forgiven people, never as a people who had forgotten sin. And the phrase 'in addition to' in verses 6, 11 and 39 taught that nothing replaced the daily offering; festivals were added on top of steady, ordinary faithfulness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter is prescription, but prescription for Israel under the Sinai covenant, bound to a priesthood, an altar and a land. The New Testament treats these feasts as 'a shadow of the things to come,' Colossians 2:16-17, and Hebrews 10:1-4 says the yearly sacrifices could never take away sins. Christians therefore do not keep this calendar as law, and no one may judge them for not keeping it.

What carries over is the shape beneath the rules. God's people still gather at set times rather than only when they feel like it. Worship still begins with cleansing and moves to joy. Generous giving to God is still ordered and not left to chance. And the church still lives by a single sacrifice for sin, now offered once, Hebrews 10:12, so that its festivals are thanksgiving, not further atonement. The 'sacrifice of praise' of Hebrews 13:15 and the living sacrifice of Romans 12:1 are the new covenant form of the offerings counted here.

debates.question: Why does the number of bulls fall by one each day across the seven days of Tabernacles?

views.label: The seventy bulls stand for the nations
views.case: The seven daily totals, thirteen down to seven, add up to exactly seventy, the traditional count of the nations listed in the table of Genesis 10. Rabbinic tradition in the Talmud read the bulls as offered on behalf of the seventy nations, and some Christian interpreters have seen in this a hint that Israel's feast looked out to the world. Zechariah 14:16, which pictures the nations keeping Tabernacles, gives the idea some canonical support.

views.label: A countdown to seven, with no stated symbol
views.case: Others note that the text itself explains nothing, and that the clearest effect of the decrease is that the seventh day lands on seven bulls, drawing attention to the number of completion before the one bull of the eighth day. On this view the total of seventy is a result of the countdown rather than its purpose, and readers should be cautious about building doctrine on numbers the passage does not interpret.

debates.bearing: Both views agree that the count is deliberate and that the feast was the richest week of Israel's year. The link to the nations is possible and fits the wider hope of Scripture, but it should be held as an inference. What the text plainly teaches is ordered, generous, complete worship, with a sin offering every day.

debates.question: Do the autumn feasts of Numbers 29 map onto events still to come at Christ's return?

views.label: A prophetic calendar still being fulfilled
views.case: Some interpreters observe that the spring feasts found their fulfilment at Christ's first coming: 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' 1 Corinthians 5:7; He is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20; and the Spirit came at Pentecost. They read the autumn feasts as awaiting the second coming: the trumpet of 1 Thessalonians 4:16, the national mourning of Zechariah 12:10, and God dwelling with His people, Revelation 21:3.

views.label: Christ fulfils the whole calendar already
views.case: Others answer that the New Testament applies the autumn feasts to Christ's first coming too. Hebrews 9:25-26 treats the Day of Atonement as fulfilled at the cross, and John 7:37-39 presents Jesus as the fulfilment of Tabernacles during His ministry. Colossians 2:16-17 calls every feast a shadow of Christ without dividing them into two sets. On this view, the future hope is real, but it is the consummation of what Christ has already done, not a separate timetable.

debates.bearing: The New Testament speaks of both a finished work and a coming completion. Atonement is accomplished once for all, while the great ingathering and God's full dwelling with His people are still ahead. Readers can see the autumn feasts pointing forward without turning them into a precise chart of end time events.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 1 literally calls the first day of the month 'a day of teruah for you.' Leviticus 23:24 names it a zikkaron teruah, a 'memorial of blowing,' which the BSB renders 'announced by trumpet blasts.' The idea of memorial matters. Numbers 10:9-10 says the trumpets were blown so that Israel would be 'remembered before the LORD' and would 'serve as a reminder for you before your God.' The blast was a summons to God's people and, in the language of the covenant, a plea that God would remember them.

Each feast day is a miqra qodesh, 'a sacred assembly,' verses 1, 7 and 12. Miqra comes from qara, to call or proclaim, and Leviticus 23:2 speaks of feasts 'you are to proclaim as sacred assemblies.' The day is holy because God has called His people together on it.

The eighth day of verse 35 is different. It is an atseret, a 'solemn assembly,' from atsar, to hold back or restrain. The word marks the closing day of Unleavened Bread in Deuteronomy 16:8 and Solomon's eighth day in 2 Chronicles 7:9, and in Joel 1:14 a related form stands beside a fast. The sense seems to be a gathering held back, a final day on which the people remain before God before going home.

The chapter carefully distinguishes two kinds of rest. On the feast days Israel must not do 'any regular work,' melekhet avodah, literally 'work of labour,' verses 1, 12 and 35. On the tenth day the phrase is stronger: 'you must not do any work,' verse 7, with no qualifier. Leviticus 23:31 repeats that difference, 'you are not to do any work at all.' Exodus 12:16 shows that on a feast day meals could still be prepared, but the Day of Atonement was a complete rest.

The phrase 'humble yourselves' in verse 7 is literally 'afflict your souls,' as the BSB footnote gives it, using nephesh, the whole living self. Psalm 35:13 pairs the same verb with fasting, 'I humbled myself with fasting,' which is why the day became known as 'the Fast,' Acts 27:9.

Every burnt offering is a reach nichoach, 'a pleasing aroma,' verses 2, 8, 13 and 36. Nichoach is related to nuach, to rest, and the phrase first appears after the flood, Genesis 8:21, when God smells Noah's offering and promises never again to curse the ground. Paul borrows the language when he says Christ gave Himself up 'as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2.

Finally, the grain and drink offerings are to be given 'according to the number prescribed,' literally 'by their number according to the ordinance,' kammishpat. The same wording returns when Ezra 3:4 records the exiles offering 'based on the number prescribed for each day,' and in Nehemiah 8:18 the eighth day is held 'according to the ordinance.' Israel's restored worship was measured by this very chapter.

typology.type: The yearly Day of Atonement, Numbers 29:7-11
typology.fulfillment: Once a year Israel fasted and the high priest carried blood into the Most Holy Place, Hebrews 9:7, and every year the day had to come round again. Hebrews reads that repetition as the sign of its limit: those sacrifices were 'an annual reminder of sins,' Hebrews 10:3. Christ entered the true sanctuary 'once for all by His own blood,' Hebrews 9:12, and then sat down, Hebrews 10:12, because nothing remained to be offered. The type falls short at its heart, since 'it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins,' Hebrews 10:4.

typology.type: The Feast of Tabernacles, God providing in the wilderness, Numbers 29:12
typology.fulfillment: The booths recalled that God 'made the Israelites dwell in booths' when He brought them out of Egypt, Leviticus 23:43, and He dwelt among them in a tent. John says the Word became flesh and 'made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14, and at this very feast Jesus offered living water to the thirsty, John 7:37-38, the gift of the Spirit, John 7:39. The escalation is from water in the desert to the Spirit within, and from a tent among the tribes to God in human flesh.

typology.type: The trumpet on the first of the seventh month, Numbers 29:1
typology.fulfillment: The blast gathered Israel and opened the holiest month of the year. The prophets took up the image of a great trumpet that gathers the scattered, Isaiah 27:13, and the New Testament speaks of 'the last trumpet' when the dead are raised, 1 Corinthians 15:52, and of 'the trumpet of God' when Christ descends, 1 Thessalonians 4:16. The shadow is a call to assemble at an earthly altar; the fulfilment is the call that gathers all God's people to Christ Himself. The correspondence is thematic rather than precise, and should not be pressed into a date.

After the seven days comes a day that stands alone, one bull and a final assembly. Many readers since the early church have seen the eighth day as a picture of new creation, the day beyond the week, and have linked it to the resurrection on the first day of a new week. The text itself does not interpret the day, so this is an inference. Yet it fits Revelation 21:3, where the feast of God dwelling with His people has no end and the multitude with palm branches 'will never again' hunger or thirst, Revelation 7:16.

study.christ:
Numbers 29 leads to Christ most clearly by contrast. The chapter is almost entirely about repetition: the same bull, ram, lamb and goat, written out again and again, and the whole cycle beginning again next year. Hebrews builds its argument on exactly this feature. If the sacrifices could cleanse, 'would not the offerings have ceased?' Hebrews 10:2. Christ 'does not need to offer daily sacrifices,' Hebrews 7:27; 'by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified,' Hebrews 10:14. The long lists of this chapter are the backdrop against which the words 'once for all' shine.

It leads to Christ by pattern. Each day's goat is 'a sin offering to make atonement for you,' verse 5, set beside burnt offerings that are 'a pleasing aroma to the LORD.' In Christ the two are joined in one person: 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and Paul describes His self giving as 'a fragrant sacrificial offering to God,' Ephesians 5:2. Cleansing and delight are no longer two animals on one altar but one obedient life laid down.

It leads to Christ by fulfilment of the feast itself. John sets a long section of his Gospel at Tabernacles, John 7:2. On 'the last and greatest day' Jesus stood and cried, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink,' John 7:37. The feast remembered water from the rock and looked forward, in Zechariah 14:8 and 14:16, to living water flowing from Jerusalem and the nations coming up to worship. Jesus claims to be the source of that water, and John explains that He meant the Spirit, John 7:39. Soon after, at the same feast, He says, 'I am the light of the world,' John 8:12.

The palm branches of the feast, Leviticus 23:40, reappear when crowds greet Jesus with Psalm 118, 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord,' John 12:13, a psalm long sung at the festivals. And they appear again in Revelation 7:9, in the hands of a multitude from every nation standing before the Lamb.

Some care is needed. The count of bulls, the measures of flour and the rams are not each a hidden picture of Jesus. The link to Christ rests on what the New Testament itself says about the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles, and on the plain logic of a sacrifice that must be repeated. The chapter shows a people who needed cleansing every day and a feast that longed for God to dwell with them. Christ is both the final sacrifice and the dwelling of God among us.
study.god:
The chapter first shows God as the Lord of time. The word for the 'appointed times' of verse 39, moedim, is the word used in Genesis 1:14 for the lights that mark 'seasons and days and years.' The God who set the sun and moon in their courses also sets the rhythm of His people's worship. Israel's year was not organised around kings or battles but around meetings with Him.

He is holy, and His holiness does not take a holiday. Every day of the feast, even the most joyful, includes 'one male goat as a sin offering,' verses 16, 19, 22, 25, 28, 31, 34 and 38. God does not ask His people to pretend that sin has gone away while they celebrate. He provides for it, daily, so that they can celebrate before Him without fear.

He is also a God of abundance who wants His people glad. Deuteronomy 16:15 says of this same feast, 'so that your joy will be complete.' The sheer scale of the offerings in Numbers 29, seventy bulls in a week, speaks of a God who is worthy of lavish honour and who gives lavishly in return, for the vow, freewill and peace offerings of verse 39 were shared as meals by the worshippers. The feast was a meal in the presence of God, Deuteronomy 12:7.

He holds together humbling and rejoicing without confusing them. The tenth day called for affliction of soul and complete rest; five days later came a week of feasting. The order matters. Cleansing comes before celebration, and the joy of the feast is the joy of a people whose sins have been dealt with, 'you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD,' Leviticus 16:30.

He is faithful to His word across the generations. The same numbers, 'according to the number prescribed,' were followed by exiles returning centuries later, Ezra 3:4, showing that God's instructions were not arbitrary but a stable way of meeting Him. And He is a God who remembers. The trumpet blast was 'a reminder for you before your God,' Numbers 10:10.

For worship, the chapter teaches that God deserves our best and our regular, that worship should be ordered and not careless, and that the gladness of God's people rests on His provision for their sin. Christians who gather around one sacrifice offered once for all have even more reason for the joy this feast was meant to hold.

crossReferences.note: The fuller calendar for the seventh month. Leviticus supplies what Numbers assumes: the meaning of each day, the penalty for failing to humble oneself on the tenth day, and the command to live in booths and wave branches. Numbers adds the precise count of animals. Read together, they give both the why and the how of the autumn feasts.

The rite behind verse 11's 'sin offering of atonement.' Leviticus 16 describes the high priest's entry behind the veil and the goat that carried Israel's sins into the wilderness, and promises 'you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD.' Numbers 29:7-11 lists the public offerings that stood alongside that central rite.

The trumpets of the feasts were a 'reminder for you before your God,' and in battle they meant Israel would be 'remembered before the LORD.' This explains why the first day of the seventh month was marked by a blast: it was a day of remembrance, calling Israel to attention and calling on God to remember His covenant.

Moses' second word on Tabernacles stresses who rejoices and why. Sons, daughters, servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans and widows all share the feast, and its goal is 'so that your joy will be complete.' Numbers gives the altar's portion; Deuteronomy shows the table spread for the whole community.

When the exiles returned, they gathered in the seventh month, rebuilt the altar, kept Tabernacles, and offered 'burnt offerings daily based on the number prescribed for each day.' Even before the temple foundation was laid, they reached for this chapter. Restored worship began by doing what Numbers 29 had required.

On discovering in the Law that Israel should dwell in booths, the people built them across Jerusalem and celebrated with 'great rejoicing.' Ezra read the Law each day, and on the eighth day they held an assembly 'according to the ordinance,' following the pattern set in Numbers 29:35.

The prophet pictures survivors from the nations going up year after year to worship the King and keep the Feast of Tabernacles. The same chapter promises living water flowing from Jerusalem, Zechariah 14:8. The feast of Numbers 29, once Israel's alone, becomes the feast of the nations.

On the last and greatest day of this feast Jesus invites the thirsty to come to Him and drink, promising streams of living water. John explains He was speaking of the Spirit. The feast that remembered God's provision in the wilderness finds its fulfilment in the gift Christ gives.

Hebrews argues from the very repetition Numbers 29 displays. Sacrifices 'offered year after year' could never perfect worshipers; they were 'an annual reminder of sins.' The yearly Day of Atonement proves that a better sacrifice was needed, one that would not have to be repeated.

A multitude from every nation stands before the Lamb holding palm branches, the emblem of Tabernacles, and God 'will spread His tabernacle over them.' They will never hunger or thirst, and the Lamb leads them to springs of living water. The feast's imagery becomes the picture of eternal rest.

study.oneStory:
In the beginning God set lights in the sky to mark 'seasons and days and years,' Genesis 1:14. Numbers 29 shows that same Creator shaping a redeemed people's year so that time itself becomes a way back to Him. After the fall, humanity lost the garden where God walked with them. At Sinai God came to dwell in a tent among Israel, and here He appoints the days on which the whole nation gathers to that tent.

The chapter answers the problem the earlier story raised. A holy God lives among sinners, so He provides cleansing, a sin offering every feast day and a great Day of Atonement every year. It also answers the wilderness story. The generation that grumbled for food and water died in the desert; their children receive a calendar of harvest feasts, a promise that they will reap what they did not sow.

Yet the chapter also leaves an ache. The offerings never stop. The same Day of Atonement comes back every autumn. Israel later kept these feasts at Solomon's temple, lost them in exile, and restored them in Ezra's day, but every restoration still needed next year's goat. The prophets looked for more: a day when living water would flow from Jerusalem and the nations would come up to keep Tabernacles, Zechariah 14:8 and 14:16.

In Christ the calendar reaches its goal. He offers Himself once for all, Hebrews 9:26, fulfilling what the tenth day could only rehearse. He stands in the temple at Tabernacles and offers the Spirit as living water, John 7:37-39. The feasts are now a shadow whose substance is Christ, Colossians 2:17.

The story ends in the new creation, where the Feast of Tabernacles never closes. John sees a numberless crowd with palm branches, sheltered by God's own tabernacle, led by the Lamb to springs of living water, Revelation 7:9-17. 'The dwelling place of God is with man,' Revelation 21:3. The eighth day of Numbers 29 was a brief final assembly before the people went home. In the new creation, God's people are at home, and the assembly goes on for ever.

quiz.q: What were the Israelites commanded to do on the tenth day of the seventh month, according to verse 7?

options.text: Hold a sacred assembly, humble themselves, and do no work.

questions: The trumpet blast called Israel to attention at the start of the sacred month. What in your own life currently serves as a wake-up call to renewed attention toward God?
The tenth day required Israel to humble themselves honestly before God. Where do you need to practice that kind of honest humbling rather than presenting a polished version of yourself to Him?
The Feast of Tabernacles combined real joy with ongoing atonement offerings every single day. Where might you need to hold celebration and repentance together rather than treating them as opposites?
Jesus stood on the last day of this very feast and offered Himself as living water to anyone who thirsts. What are you currently thirsting for that only He can truly satisfy?

This whole sacred calendar had to be repeated every single year, never finally finishing the work of atonement. How does resting in Christ's one, final sacrifice change the way you approach your own sense of needing to atone for yourself?

translationNotes.note: This chapter never names the tenth day as Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement; that name and its fuller ritual, including the scapegoat, comes from Leviticus 16 and 23, which this passage assumes its readers already know.

The Feast of Tabernacles, Sukkot, involved living in temporary shelters for seven days, commemorating Israel's wilderness journey, Leviticus 23:42-43, a detail not repeated in this chapter's purely sacrificial instructions.

The eighth day, described as a solemn assembly distinct from the preceding seven, is called Shemini Atzeret in later Jewish tradition and is treated in the Hebrew text as its own separate, smaller festival rather than simply the feast's final day.
